newsitem.title: PERU: Most Peruvians think MRTA lying about tunnel -poll.
newsitem.headline: Most Peruvians think MRTA lying about tunnel -poll.

text.p: Most Peruvians believe Marxist rebels holding 72 VIPs lied when they claimed security forces were building a tunnel under the Japanese ambassador's home to rescue the hostages, a poll made public on Sunday said.

A survey taken following the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's allegation on Thursday that led to a suspension of peace talks showed 56 percent of Peruvians believed no tunnel existed, according to a leading local pollster, Compania Peruana de Investigacion de Mercados (CPI).
A further 31 percent said there was a tunnel and 13 percent held no opinion, the poll released on local television said.
The MRTA suspended talks aimed at reaching a bloodless solution to the 11-week-old siege alleging the government was planning to use a tunnel in an attack on the diplomatic residence.

Defence Minister Tomas Castillo Meza denied the existence of a tunnel, but some security force sources told Reuters at least four tunnels have been built while music was blasted from loudspeakers around the residence.
Local media has generally reported that a tunnel has been constructed as part of a plan to attack the residence should the government choose to end the crisis by force.

Among a variety of reasons offered to explain why the MRTA had held up further talks was that the group was not achieving its main aim of the release of up to 400 jailed comrades. This belief was held by 18 percent of those polled.
Other popular explanations included the belief the rebels were trying to pressure the government and that they wanted to gain publicity.
The CPI poll also showed an overwhelming 76 percent still believed the government should try to end the crisis through dialogue, while only 22 percent thought a military option should be used.
The poll's error of margin was not known nor how many people were surveyed by CPI, which usually conducts polls of up to 500 people in the capital of Lima.

The MRTA agreed earlier on Sunday to return to the negotiating table on Monday. The rebels originally took hundreds of hostages on Dec. 17 when it stormed a cocktail party but most captives were freed in the first few weeks of the siege.
